title: Crash recovery (ARIES)
summary: How a steal, no-force database survives crashes: LSNs on pages and log records, fuzzy checkpoints, the analysis, redo and undo passes, and compensation log records that make recovery safe to repeat.
outcomes: Explain why steal requires undo and no-force requires redo, and how the WAL rule makes both possible
Use pageLSN, recLSN, flushedLSN and lastLSN to decide whether a page may be written or an update must be redone
Rebuild the transaction and dirty page tables in an analysis pass and compute where redo starts
Trace undo with CLRs and UndoNextLSN, including a second crash during recovery
Explain why ARIES repeats history for losers instead of redoing only committed work

lessons.title: Why a crash needs both undo and redo

blocks.md:
From the prerequisite courses you know the two halves of the setup: a **buffer pool** caches disk pages in memory and evicts dirty ones, and a **write-ahead log (WAL)** records every change and is made durable with fsync. Databases built this way update pages **in place**: a modified page goes back to the same disk location it was read from.

A crash (power loss, kernel panic, process kill) wipes the buffer pool. What survives is the disk copy of each page plus the part of the log that already reached stable storage. **Crash recovery** is the code that runs at restart to turn that leftover state into a correct one: every committed transaction fully present, every uncommitted one fully gone.

How hard recovery is depends on two buffer pool rules, as defined in the ARIES paper (Mohan et al., 1992), which takes the terms from Haerder and Reuter (1983):

- **Steal**: the buffer pool may write a page to disk while it holds changes of a transaction that has not committed yet. **No-steal** forbids that.
- **Force**: a transaction may not commit until every page it modified is written to disk. **No-force** lets it commit with its pages still dirty in memory.

Steal means disk can hold uncommitted data, so recovery must be able to **undo**. No-force means disk can miss committed data, so recovery must be able to **redo**.

blocks.title: Steal and no-force leave the disk wrong in both directions

scenes.caption: Both transactions update pages in the buffer pool. Each update also appends a log record to the in-memory log buffer.
Steal: memory is tight, so the buffer pool evicts a page that holds an uncommitted change of T2. Disk now contains data that may never commit.
No-force: T1 commits by forcing only its log records to disk. Its modified page stays dirty in memory, so the data pages on disk lack a committed change.
Crash: everything volatile is gone. Disk has T2 data that must be undone and misses T1 data that must be redone. Only the log can tell recovery which is which.

blocks.title: What recovery must do under each buffer policy

scenes.caption: Each cell counts the recovery actions needed: undo, redo, both (2) or neither (0). No-steal plus force needs neither, because disk only ever holds committed data.
Steal alone forces undo; no-force alone forces redo. Each relaxation buys runtime freedom and costs one recovery mechanism.
ARIES targets the hardest cell, steal plus no-force, because it gives the buffer pool and commit path the most freedom at runtime.

blocks.md: Why accept the hard cell? No-steal means a transaction's whole write set must stay pinned in memory until commit, and the ARIES paper notes that with record-level locking a page that always holds some uncommitted update might then never be written at all. Force means every commit waits for random writes of every page it touched, instead of one sequential append to the log. The figure below is a deliberately simple cost model of that second point.

blocks.title: Commit latency: force pages versus force only the log

scenes.caption: Simplified model: force pays one random write per modified page, done one after another, plus the commit log flush; no-force pays only the log flush. Both costs are illustrative slider values, not measurements.
Even with fast random writes the force line still grows with transaction size, while the no-force line stays flat. Real systems also batch commits (group commit), widening the gap.

blocks.md:
Both rules lean on the WAL protocol, which ARIES keeps exactly:

1. **Log before data**: a dirty page may be written to disk only after the log records describing its changes are on stable storage. This makes undo possible after a steal.
2. **Log at commit**: a transaction counts as committed only once its commit record and everything before it are on stable storage. This makes redo possible under no-force.

The rest of this course is about the bookkeeping that lets recovery apply those log records precisely, and survive crashing again in the middle of recovery.
Steal creates the need for **undo**, no-force creates the need for **redo**. ARIES allows both, so it must do both, using only the log and a little state stored on each page.

blocks.question: A system uses no-steal and no-force. After a crash, which work can recovery skip entirely?
options: Redo of committed transactions, because their pages were written at commit
Undo of uncommitted transactions, because their changes never reached the data pages
Both, because the log already contains everything
Neither, because the log may be incomplete
blocks.explain: No-steal guarantees no uncommitted change was ever written to a data page, so there is nothing to undo. No-force means committed changes may still be missing on disk, so redo is still required.

blocks.question: Under steal, the buffer pool wants to evict a page whose newest change is described by a log record still sitting in the in-memory log buffer. What must happen first?
options: Nothing, the page can be written right away
The transaction that made the change must commit
The log must be flushed at least up to that record
The page must be copied to a shadow location
blocks.explain: Write-ahead logging: before a page goes to disk, the log records for its changes must be stable. Otherwise a crash could leave an uncommitted change on disk with no log record to undo it.

lessons.title: LSNs, pageLSN and the two tables recovery rebuilds

blocks.md:
ARIES ties everything to the **log sequence number (LSN)**. Every log record gets one when it is appended, and LSNs only increase. In the paper an LSN is simply the address of the record's first byte in the ever-growing log, so comparing two LSNs tells you which record came first.

We will use round numbers (10, 20, 30, ...) so the examples are easy to follow.

An **update log record** carries these fields (ARIES paper, section 4.1):

- `LSN`, `Type` (update, compensation, commit, ...) and `TransID`
- `PrevLSN`: the previous record written by the same transaction, so each transaction's records form a backward linked list (0 for its first record)
- `PageID`: the page the update touched
- `Data`: enough to redo the change and to undo it, for example the before and after values of a field

Records may be physical (byte images) or operational (add 5 to field 3). Our examples use before and after values.

Four more LSN-valued fields connect the log to everything else:

- **pageLSN**, stored inside every data page: the LSN of the newest log record applied to that page.
- **flushedLSN**, in memory: the last LSN known to be on stable storage.
- **lastLSN**, per transaction: its newest log record.
- **recLSN**, per dirty page: roughly the first log record that dirtied the page since it was last written to disk. The paper records the end-of-log LSN at the moment the clean page is first fixed for update, which is the same point.

The last two live in the **Active Transaction Table (ATT)** and the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)**.

blocks.title: The running example: ten log records and three pages

scenes.caption: Three transactions update pages P1, P2 and P3, which hold values A=100, B=50, C=7. A checkpoint (BEGCK, ENDCK) sits at LSN 30 and 40. T1 commits at 70 and ends at 90.
T1 changes A on P1 from 100 to 90. The update writes LSN 10 into P1, so P1 now says: I reflect the log up to 10.
T2 changes B on P2 from 50 to 60. P2 gets pageLSN 20.
T1 changes C on P3 from 7 to 8 at LSN 50. Its PrevLSN is 10, linking it to T1's earlier record.

T2 changes A on P1 from 90 to 95 at LSN 60; P1 pageLSN jumps from 10 to 60. Simplified: T1 locks A until it commits at 70, so a real T2 would wait or change another record on P1. Reusing A keeps the numbers small.
T3 changes B on P2 from 60 to 40 at LSN 80. Two uncommitted transactions have now touched P2.
T2 changes C on P3 from 8 to 12 at LSN 100. Then the system crashes. Lesson 4 recovers from exactly this log.

blocks.tex: \text{write page } x \text{ to disk only if } \mathit{pageLSN}(x) \le \mathit{flushedLSN}
blocks.caption: The WAL rule in LSN form. If it does not hold, the buffer pool first forces the log up to pageLSN(x).

blocks.prompt: In our example the buffer pool stole P1 (writing T2's uncommitted A=95 to disk) at some moment after LSN 60 and before the crash. What is the smallest flushedLSN that the WAL rule allows at that moment?
blocks.reveal: **60.** P1's pageLSN is 60, so the log must be stable at least through LSN 60 before P1 can be written. That guarantees the record needed to undo T2's change (before value 90) survives any crash that follows.

blocks.md:
The two tables summarize what is in flight:

- **ATT**: one entry per transaction that has not written its end record, with its status and lastLSN. lastLSN is where undo would start for that transaction.
- **DPT**: one entry per dirty page in the buffer pool, with its recLSN. The smallest recLSN is the oldest log position whose effect might be missing on disk.

Both tables live in memory, so a crash destroys them. Restart rebuilds them from the last checkpoint plus the log. A small **master record** at a fixed disk location stores the LSN of the last complete checkpoint so restart knows where to begin.

Do not mix up pageLSN and recLSN. In the example, P1 was first dirtied at LSN 10 and last changed at 60, so its recLSN is 10 while its pageLSN is 60. recLSN says where redo for the page might need to start; pageLSN says which changes the page already contains.

blocks.question: flushedLSN is 40. The buffer pool picks P3 for eviction; its pageLSN is 50 and its recLSN is 50. What does a correct buffer pool do?
options: Write P3 now, since recLSN 50 is greater than flushedLSN
Force the log through at least LSN 50, then write P3
Refuse to evict P3 until the transaction that wrote LSN 50 commits
Write P3 and lower its pageLSN to 40
blocks.explain: The WAL rule compares pageLSN with flushedLSN: 50 is greater than 40, so the log must be forced through 50 first. Waiting for commit is the no-steal rule, which ARIES does not need.

blocks.question: Why does each page carry its own pageLSN instead of the DBMS just remembering which pages were flushed?
options: The pageLSN is written atomically with the page, so after a crash the disk copy itself says which logged updates it already contains
It saves memory in the buffer pool
It lets the log be deleted after every checkpoint
It replaces the need for the Dirty Page Table
blocks.explain: Any in-memory record of flushes is lost in the crash, and logging every flush would cost extra writes. The pageLSN travels with the page, so redo can compare it with a log record's LSN and know for sure whether that update is present.

lessons.title: Commit, abort with CLRs, and fuzzy checkpoints

blocks.md:
Recovery is half restart code and half discipline during normal operation. Three normal-time actions matter.

**Commit.** The transaction appends a COMMIT record and the log is forced through it; only then is the client told the transaction committed. Later a TXN-END record is appended to say the transaction will write nothing more. TXN-END does not need to be forced (CMU 15-445 notes). The data pages are not touched by commit at all: that is no-force.

blocks.title: T1 commits while P1 waits in the buffer pool

scenes.caption: T1 updates C on P3. The log manager assigns LSN 50, and P3 gets pageLSN 50 while still only in memory.
T1 commits. Its COMMIT record (LSN 70) and everything before it are forced to disk in one sequential write. Then the client hears success.
TXN-END (LSN 90) is appended lazily; nobody waits for it. P3 is still dirty in memory, which is fine because the log can redo it.
Later the buffer pool evicts P1, whose pageLSN is 60. Since flushedLSN 70 is at least 60, the WAL rule allows the write even though T2 has not committed: a steal.

blocks.md:
**Abort.** To roll back, the DBMS appends an ABORT record, then walks the transaction's PrevLSN chain backward, undoing each update. For every update it undoes, it writes a **compensation log record (CLR)** that describes the undo as a new change. A CLR has one extra field, **UndoNextLSN**: the PrevLSN of the record it compensates, meaning the next record still to be undone. When the chain reaches 0 it writes TXN-END.

CLRs are **redo-only**: they contain no undo information and are never undone themselves.

blocks.title: Rolling back T5: each undo becomes a CLR

scenes.caption: T5 updated A, B and C at LSN 1 to 3, chained by PrevLSN (0, 1, 2). Then it decides to abort and appends ABORT at LSN 4.
Undo starts at the newest update, LSN 3. Restoring C writes CLR at LSN 5 whose UndoNextLSN is 2, the PrevLSN of record 3.
Next is LSN 2: restore B, write CLR at LSN 6 pointing to 1.
Then LSN 1: restore A, CLR at LSN 7 with UndoNextLSN 0, meaning nothing is left to undo. TXN-END at LSN 8 closes the transaction.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the system crashed right after CLR 6 reached disk, before CLR 7. At restart, how does ARIES know where T5's rollback should resume, and could it undo C a second time?
blocks.reveal: It reads T5's last record, CLR 6, and follows its **UndoNextLSN = 1**. Only record 1 is left to undo. Records 3 and 2 are skipped because the CLRs already account for them, so C and B are never undone twice. The paper's claim is that each update gets **at most one CLR**, no matter how many times restart is repeated.

blocks.md:
**Checkpoints.** Without them, restart would have to scan the log from the very beginning. ARIES uses a **fuzzy checkpoint** that does not stop transactions:

1. Write a BEGIN-CHECKPOINT record.
2. Build an END-CHECKPOINT record holding copies of the ATT and DPT, and append it. Transactions keep running meanwhile.
3. Once END-CHECKPOINT is on stable storage, store the BEGIN-CHECKPOINT LSN in the master record.

If the crash comes between steps 1 and 3, the checkpoint is incomplete and restart uses the previous one. ARIES does **not** flush dirty pages during a checkpoint; the buffer pool keeps writing them in the background, which is what lets redo start late in the log.

A checkpoint is not a point where the disk is consistent. A fuzzy checkpoint only records which transactions were active and which pages were dirty. Redo usually has to start **before** the checkpoint, at the smallest recLSN in the DPT, because a page dirtied long ago may still be unflushed.

blocks.question: Why may a CLR never itself be undone?
options: CLRs are always forced to disk, so they are permanent
CLRs belong to the system, not to a transaction
CLRs are deleted at the next checkpoint
Undoing a CLR would reinstate the original change, and a rollback in progress must only move backward
blocks.explain: A CLR records progress of a rollback. Undoing it would reinstate an uncommitted change. Making CLRs redo-only and chaining them with UndoNextLSN guarantees rollbacks only move toward the start of the transaction.

blocks.question: The last checkpoint began at LSN 30, and its DPT lists P1 with recLSN 10. Where must the redo pass start, at the latest?
options: LSN 30, the BEGIN-CHECKPOINT
LSN 40, the END-CHECKPOINT
LSN 10, the smallest recLSN
LSN 0, the start of the log
blocks.explain: P1 has been dirty since LSN 10 and may never have been written, so updates from LSN 10 onward might be missing on disk. Starting at 30 would lose them. Starting at 0 is safe but wasteful.

lessons.title: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history

blocks.md:
ARIES restart runs three passes over the log, in this order:

1. **Analysis** scans forward from the last checkpoint and rebuilds the ATT and DPT as they were at the crash.
2. **Redo** scans forward from the smallest recLSN and reapplies every logged change that might be missing, for all transactions, including ones that will be rolled back. The paper calls this **repeating history**.
3. **Undo** walks backward and rolls back every transaction that was still active at the crash, the **losers**.

Each pass covers a different stretch of the log.

blocks.title: Which part of the log each pass touches

scenes.caption: The log from the running example, LSN 10 to 100, with the checkpoint at 30 and 40. The crash happens right after LSN 100.
Analysis starts at BEGIN-CHECKPOINT (30) and reads to the end of the log.
Redo starts earlier, at the smallest recLSN (10), because P1 has been dirty since then. It also reads to the end.
Undo goes backward from the newest loser record (100) down to the oldest one (20, T2's first update). Its reach depends on how old the oldest loser is.

blocks.md:
**Analysis rules** (CMU 15-445 notes, matching the paper's pseudocode). Start from the END-CHECKPOINT tables, then for each later record:

- Any record of a transaction not in the ATT adds it with status U (undo candidate). Each record updates its lastLSN.
- COMMIT sets status C. TXN-END removes the transaction.
- An update or CLR for a page not in the DPT adds the page with recLSN equal to this record's LSN.

At the end, transactions still marked U are the losers, and RedoLSN is the smallest recLSN.

blocks.title: Analysis pass on the running example

scenes.caption: Restart reads the master record: last complete checkpoint began at LSN 30. Analysis starts with empty tables and scans forward from there.
END-CHECKPOINT: copy its ATT (T1 lastLSN 10, T2 lastLSN 20) and DPT (P1 recLSN 10, P2 recLSN 20). Both transactions start with status U, a candidate for undo.
T1 updates P3. T1 lastLSN becomes 50. P3 is not in the DPT, so it is added with recLSN 50: it might be dirty and unflushed.
T2 updates P1, which is already in the DPT, so its recLSN stays 10. T2 lastLSN becomes 60.
COMMIT for T1: status becomes C. T1 will not be undone.
T3 was not in the checkpoint; its first record adds it to the ATT with lastLSN 80. P2 already has recLSN 20.
TXN-END for T1: remove it from the ATT. It is completely finished.
T2 updates P3: lastLSN 100. End of log. Losers are T2 and T3, and redo will start at the smallest recLSN, 10.

blocks.md: The DPT from analysis is conservative. It still lists P1 with recLSN 10 even though P1 was written to disk after LSN 60, because no log record mentions that write. Redo resolves such doubts by reading the page and checking its pageLSN.

**Redo rules.** Scan forward from RedoLSN. For each update or CLR, reapply it unless one of these holds (CMU notes; paper Fig. 11):

- the page is not in the DPT (it was clean at the crash),
- the record's LSN is below the page's recLSN (that change was flushed before the page got dirty again),
- the page's on-disk pageLSN is at least the record's LSN (the change is already there; this check needs a page read).

A redone change sets pageLSN to the record's LSN. Redo writes **no** log records.

blocks.title: Redo pass, record by record

scenes.caption: Disk state at the crash: P1 holds A=95 with pageLSN 60 (stolen), P2 holds B=60 with pageLSN 20 (written back after the checkpoint, before LSN 80), P3 was never written: C=7, pageLSN 0. Redo starts at RedoLSN 10.
LSN 10 (T1 on P1): P1 is in the DPT and 10 is at least recLSN 10, so fetch P1. Its pageLSN 60 is at least 10: the change is already on disk. Skip.
LSN 20 (T2 on P2): fetch P2. pageLSN 20 equals the record LSN, so the change is present. Skip.
LSN 50 (T1 on P3): P3 on disk has pageLSN 0, less than 50. Redo: C becomes 8, pageLSN 50.
LSN 60 (T2 on P1): P1 pageLSN is 60, so this change was in the stolen page. Skip. Note it belongs to a loser, and the check does not care.
LSN 80 (T3 on P2): pageLSN 20 is less than 80. Redo it, although T3 is a loser: B becomes 40, pageLSN 80.
LSN 100 (T2 on P3): pageLSN 50 is less than 100. Redo: C becomes 12. The database now matches the moment of the crash exactly.

blocks.md: Redo is decided per page by LSN comparison alone, never by whether the transaction committed. Updates 80 and 100 belong to losers and are redone anyway. After redo the database is exactly as it was at the crash, and only then does undo begin.

Two refinements from the paper. If a page turns out to already hold the change, ARIES may raise that page's recLSN to pageLSN + 1, so later records for it are skipped without another page check. And because each page's updates are independent, redo can prefetch every DPT page with parallel I/O and replay per-page queues in parallel, as long as each page's records are applied in log order.

blocks.question: Redo reaches LSN 60 (T2's update of P1). The DPT says P1 recLSN 10, and P1 read from disk has pageLSN 60. What happens?
options: Redo it, because 60 is at least recLSN 10
Skip it, because T2 is a loser
Skip it, because the page's pageLSN shows the change is already on disk
Undo it immediately, because the page holds uncommitted data
blocks.explain: Passing the recLSN test only means the change might be missing. Reading the page settles it: pageLSN 60 means this update is already there. Loser status plays no role in redo, and undo waits for the undo pass.

blocks.question: Which statement about the redo pass is true?
options: It may read pages whose changes turn out to be on disk already
It writes a log record for every update it reapplies
It only reapplies changes of committed transactions
It starts at the BEGIN-CHECKPOINT record
blocks.explain: The DPT over-approximates, so some fetched pages (P1 and P2 here) need nothing. Redo logs nothing, repeats loser changes too, and starts at the smallest recLSN, which can be before the checkpoint.

lessons.title: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery

blocks.title: Undo pass on the running example

scenes.caption: After redo: A=95, B=40, C=12, the crash state. Losers T2 (undo next 100) and T3 (undo next 80). Undo always takes the largest pending LSN across all losers.
Largest pending LSN is 100 (T2). Restore C to 8 and write CLR 110 with UndoNextLSN 60. T2 now waits at 60, T3 at 80.
Largest is now 80 (T3). Restore B to 60, write CLR 120 with UndoNextLSN 0. T3 has nothing left, so TXN-END 130 is written for it.
Only T2 remains, at 60. Restore A to 90, CLR 140 with UndoNextLSN 20.
Finally LSN 20: restore B to 50, CLR 150 with UndoNextLSN 0, then TXN-END 160. Result: A=90 and C=8 from committed T1, B=50 as before any loser touched it.

blocks.prompt: Now suppose the machine crashes again during undo, right after CLR 140 reached disk (CLR 150 and END 160 never happened), and no page was written. On the second restart, how many CLRs will undo write?
blocks.reveal: **One.** Analysis sees CLR 110, CLR 120, T3's END at 130 and CLR 140, so only T2 is a loser, with UndoNextLSN = 20 taken from CLR 140. Redo repeats history again, now including the CLRs: it reapplies 6 records (50, 80, 100, 110, 120, 140), restoring A=90, B=60, C=8. Undo then handles only LSN 20 and writes a single CLR. Across both restarts each update got exactly one CLR, and the final state (A=90, B=50, C=8) is the same.

scenes.caption: First restart: redo scans 10 records from LSN 10 and reapplies 3; undo writes 4 CLRs (and 2 TXN-END records).
Second restart after crashing at CLR 140: the log is longer, so redo scans 14 and reapplies 6, but undo writes only 1 CLR. Work already done in undo is never repeated.

blocks.md:
**Why repeat history instead of redoing only winners?** The paper (section 10.1) shows the failure of *selective redo* with fine-grained locking. Take one page holding a counter, last written to disk at pageLSN 10 with value 100. Loser T2 logs add 5 at LSN 20, then committed T1 logs add 3 at LSN 30.

- Selective redo reapplies only LSN 30: value 103, pageLSN 30. Undo of LSN 20 then sees pageLSN 30, at least 20, assumes the add 5 is present and subtracts it: **98**. Wrong.
- Repeating history reapplies both: 108. Undo subtracts 5: **103**, the correct answer.

Once a page's pageLSN can run ahead of changes it does not contain, it stops being a true description of the page. Repeating history keeps it true.

ARIES in one line: **repeat history, then undo the losers, logging every undo as a redo-only CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips what is already undone**. That makes recovery idempotent: crash during analysis or redo and you simply start over; crash during undo and you resume where the CLRs say.

**In real systems.** Microsoft's documentation states that SQL Server's traditional recovery follows the ARIES model with analysis, redo and undo phases, and that recovery time is roughly proportional to the size of the longest transaction active at the crash, since undo must roll all of it back. Its Accelerated Database Recovery feature attacks that by versioning modifications so aborted work can be ignored instead of undone.

Redo's pageLSN test assumes a page on disk is either wholly old or wholly new. PostgreSQL's docs note that a page write interrupted by an OS crash can leave a mix of both, so with `full_page_writes` (default on) it logs a full page image on the first change of each page after a checkpoint.

Tuning tradeoffs follow directly from the passes. Rare checkpoints and slow background page writes make the smallest recLSN old, so redo scans more log. Long-running transactions make undo long and keep old log needed. Frequent checkpoints shorten redo but cost extra log and page writes at runtime.

blocks.question: One page, all records for it. Before the crash: updates 1 and 2, the page is written to disk, updates 3 and 4, a partial rollback writes CLRs 4' and 3', then updates 5 and 6. The transaction is a loser. What does ARIES do at restart?
options: Redo nothing, since the transaction is a loser; undo 6, 5, 2, 1
Redo 1 through 6; undo 6, 5, 4', 3'
blocks.explain: This is Fig. 13 of the ARIES paper. Redo repeats everything after the page write, CLRs included. Undo follows PrevLSN from 6 to 5, then reaches CLR 3', whose UndoNextLSN points at 2, so 4 and 3 are not undone again. Then 2 and 1.

blocks.question: A database keeps very frequent fuzzy checkpoints, yet restart after a crash still takes an hour. Analysis and redo finish in seconds. What is the most likely cause?
options: The DPT was too large
Checkpoints were incomplete, so analysis started at the beginning of the log
Redo had to repeat history for loser transactions
A long-running transaction was active at the crash and undo must roll back all of its work
blocks.explain: Checkpoints bound analysis and, with good background flushing, redo. Undo is bounded only by how much work losers did. That is exactly the case Microsoft cites for long recovery and the motivation for Accelerated Database Recovery.
